key-generation.why: ID blocks avoid both collisions and per-request coordination. Hash-and-retry works with care. A single locked counter is correct but becomes the bottleneck. Three characters of base62 (238,328 codes) run out almost immediately.

fast-redirects.why: The mapping is tiny and almost immutable: ideal for caching. The database stays the source of truth.

analytics.why: Writes on the hot read path add latency and contention. Events plus async aggregation keep redirects fast; the requirement allows minutes of lag.

write-rate.why: 100,000,000 ÷ (30 × 86,400) ≈ 38.6 per second on average: writes are modest; reads are the scaling problem.

duplicate-long-url.why: It's a product decision: reuse saves space; separate links allow per-user analytics and deletion. Saying which you chose, and why, is the point.

considerations: Restated requirements and asked about custom aliases, expiry and analytics freshness
Estimated write QPS (~40/s) and read QPS (~400/s average) and the storage per year
A short-code scheme that avoids collisions (ID blocks + base62, or hash with retry) and its length
A key-value or relational table keyed by short code, with the long URL and owner
A cache on the redirect path, and 301 vs 302 chosen deliberately (302 keeps analytics accurate)
Asynchronous click analytics via events and aggregation
What happens when the cache or database is down, and how to avoid a single point of failure
